steps.instruction: In 1972, 48 male bank supervisors each reviewed one personnel file and decided whether to recommend the candidate for promotion. The files were identical except for one thing: 24 stated the candidate was male and 24 stated female. Each card in the **Original Groups** panel is one supervisor's review of a file — a filled card means that supervisor recommended promotion. A card sits in the **male** or **female** group according to the file that supervisor reviewed.
steps.observe: The supervisors recommended promotion for **21 of 24** reviews in the **male** group, but only **14 of 24** in the **female** group.

gate.question: How big is the gap between the two promotion rates?

choices.text: About 7 percentage points (21/24 vs 14/24 — only 7 files apart)

gate.feedback: 21/24 = 87.5% and 14/24 = 58.3%, a 29.2 percentage point difference. The question for the rest of this activity: could a gap that large happen just by chance?
gate.retryFeedback: Convert each count to a rate first: 21 out of 24, and 14 out of 24.

steps.instruction: The skeptic's position — the *null hypothesis* — says the file's stated sex had **no effect** on any supervisor's decision.

gate.question: If the file's stated sex truly had no effect, what would that mean about these 48 decisions?

choices.text: Exactly 50% in each group would be promoted
The same 35 supervisors would have recommended promotion regardless of the name on the file
We would need more data to tell

gate.feedback: Under the null hypothesis the decisions are fixed — the same 35 supervisors would have recommended promotion either way. Only the group labels are random. That's exactly what shuffling simulates.
gate.retryFeedback: Think about what "no effect" means: each supervisor's decision came from the candidate's qualifications, not the sex on the file — so it would be the same either way.

steps.instruction: You're about to simulate one shuffle. The **+1** button keeps the two groups at 24 and 24 but **reassigns the same 35 promotions at random** across them — the **Shuffled Groups** panel shows the result (*same values, new grouping*). **Before you click anything**, commit to a prediction.

gate.question: How big do you expect the difference in promotion rates to be in one shuffle, if only chance is at work?

choices.text: Around 29 points, like the observed difference
choices.feedback: You've committed — now click **+1** and see where the shuffle actually lands.
You've committed — now click **+1** and see where the shuffle actually lands.
You've committed — now click **+1** and see. (Watch whether chance alone produces *exactly* zero.)

steps.observe: Click **+1** a few times. Watch the same 35 promotions get reassigned to new groups, and watch where each shuffled difference lands on the chart.

steps.instruction: One shuffle is one data point. Click **+100**, then **+1000**, to see what chance alone typically produces.
steps.observe: The null distribution piles up — where is its center? Now find the red line marking the observed difference (29.2 pp).

gate.question: Look at the null distribution. Where does the observed difference fall?

choices.text: In the middle of the distribution — it looks typical for chance
Out in the tail — very few shuffles produced a difference this large
I can't tell from the chart

gate.feedback: The observed 29.2 pp gap sits far in the right tail. The p-value (shown in the results panel) is the fraction of shuffles at least that extreme — and it's small.
gate.retryFeedback: Compare the red line's position to where most of the shuffled differences piled up. Is 29.2 pp common among the shuffles?

steps.instruction: Time to conclude. The p-value in the results panel tells you how often chance alone produced a difference as large as the one observed. Before you read the conclusion, put the reasoning in your own words.

prompts.label: Why does shuffling produce a distribution centered at zero, even though the actual study's observed difference is 29.2 pp?
What does the fraction of shuffles at or beyond 29.2 pp tell us — and why is that fraction the p-value?
If we ran the shuffle again with a different random seed, would the p-value be exactly the same, roughly the same, or wildly different? Why?

respond.answer: A strong answer: shuffling enforces the null (labels don't matter), so on average the groups differ by 0 — the distribution centers at zero **by construction**, regardless of the real 29.2 pp gap. The fraction of shuffles at least as extreme as 29.2 pp **is** the p-value: how often chance alone matches the data. A different seed gives a **roughly** equal p-value (it's an estimate from finitely many shuffles); more shuffles → more stable.

steps.reveal: Because differences of 29.2 pp or more almost never occur when the promotions are reassigned at random, chance is not a plausible explanation. The data provide convincing evidence that the file's stated sex influenced the promotion decisions. Note the logic: we didn't prove discrimination directly — a small p-value makes the skeptic's "just luck" explanation implausible, though it never rules chance out completely.
